rationale: The objective asks about TSTR transfer as well as augmentation gain. decision: Resize the VAE latent and soften the KL weight
chosen: latent_dim=64, beta=0.5, batch_size=128, n_layers=3 (proposal latent_dim=32, beta=1.0, batch_size=256)
rationale: The profile's intrinsic dimension is about 50.4, and 154 PCA components are needed for 90% variance. A 32-dimensional latent sits below the estimated intrinsic dimension, so it would under-represent texture. 64 is the nearest round size above it. Gaussian-likelihood VAEs on pixels are known to blur, and beta=0.5 puts more weight on reconstruction, which sharpens samples while keeping a usable prior. Batch 128 doubles the number of updates within the 750 s cap for n of about 4,500.

The results are good enough for the main objective. Augmenting the 5% subset with DDPM samples raises macro-F1 from 0.709 to 0.764, a gain of +0.055 (95% CI [0.027, 0.080], P(gain>0)=1.0). The DDPM also clearly beats the VAE as a generator: FD is 7.2 vs 74.7 and coverage is 0.169 vs 0.006. The VAE's augmentation gain is close (+0.047, overlapping CI), but its TSTR collapses to 0.176. The DDPM's IID fidelity falls short of the real-holdout reference (recall 0.557 vs 0.967, coverage 0.169 vs 0.409, FD 7.2 vs 0.43). Against the shifted real test split it is roughly on par (coverage 0.154, FD 10.6, precision 0.834). So the generator is no further from the training distribution than genuinely new test patches are. TSTR does not reach parity: 0.639 vs 0.709 real-only, a gap of −0.070 (CI [−0.098, −0.045]). The deficit is concentrated in smooth muscle (0.27), lymphocytes (0.52) and debris (0.46). There is no sign of memorisation: DCR ratio 1.06, too-close fraction 0.7%, no exact copies. The primary metric, macro_f1_gain, is positive and its CI excludes zero. The primary model is the best available generator, and no deterministic trigger fires on it. The only trigger concerns the VAE comparison model (low diversity). Retuning the VAE (beta 0.25) cannot improve the primary metric unless it then beats the DDPM. Its augmentation gain (+0.047) is already within noise of the DDPM's, and its fidelity is an order of magnitude worse. The DDPM's main weaknesses are lower recall and coverage than the IID holdout, and a TSTR gap. They have two likely causes. First, the DDPM is under-trained: it stopped on the time cap at epoch 545 with best_epoch = final epoch, so validation loss was still improving. Second, there is a large train/test shift (Fréchet ratio 24.4), which also caps the real-only classifier. Cancer-associated stroma recall sits at about 0.33 under every condition, which points to a shift or label issue rather than a generator issue. No in-range revision can add training time, because the 1500 s cap is fixed. Lowering guidance below 1.5 to gain diversity would probably weaken class fidelity. Augmentation already suggests some class blur: lymphocyte recall fell from 0.90 to 0.78. Fidelity was evaluated on only 501 samples, and utility CIs are about ±0.027, so any plausible gain from a retune would likely be within noise. Spending compute on such a gamble is not justified.

evidence.expected_effect: No change; current results stand. Report three caveats with them. (1) The augmentation gain is about +0.055 macro-F1, robustly positive. (2) Synthetic-only training transfers but does not reach parity (−0.070 vs real-only), with weak classes being smooth muscle, lymphocytes and debris. (3) Test-split utility measures transfer under substantial train/test shift. The DDPM was time-limited and still improving, so a larger training budget is the most likely route to better recall, coverage and TSTR in a future run.
